content.theory:
A fixed-size array is great until you run out of room — then you're stuck. **ArrayList** is the go-to **resizable list** from `java.util`. It wraps an array and grows it automatically when you `add()`, which is why it's the default collection for ordered data in almost every real Java program.

Unlike arrays, an `ArrayList` needs the `import`:

```java
import java.util.*;

ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Ada");
names.add("Linus");
```

### Generics — the angle brackets

`ArrayList<String>` is pronounced "ArrayList of String". The **generic type** tells the compiler exactly what the list holds, so you get type safety — you can't accidentally insert an `int` into a `String` list. Two details trip everyone up:

- The diamond `<>` on the right side lets Java infer the type from the left.
- You can't write `ArrayList<int>` — generics need **reference types**. Use the wrapper class `ArrayList<Integer>` and Java **autoboxes** plain `int` values into `Integer` objects automatically.

### Common methods

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `add(item)` | Append to the end |
| `get(i)` | Read the element at index `i` |
| `set(i, item)` | Replace the element at index `i` |
| `remove(i)` | Delete the element at index `i` |
| `size()` | Number of elements |
| `contains(item)` | True if the list holds `item` |

### Looping and sorting

A **for-each loop** is the cleanest way to visit every element — no index math, no off-by-one errors:

```java
for (String name : names) {
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

To sort, use `Collections.sort(names)` — a static utility method that sorts any `List` of `Comparable` elements in place. Avoid a classic bug: `names.size()` returns the **count**, while `names.length` doesn't exist on an `ArrayList` (that's an array thing).

exercise.instruction: Create an ArrayList<String> named 'names'. Add the names "Ada" then "Linus". Print the size on its own line with System.out.println(names.size()), then print each name on its own line using a for-each loop over 'names'.
hints: Hint 1: import java.util.*; goes above the class — ArrayList lives there.
Hint 2: ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); then names.add("Ada"); names.add("Linus");
Hint 3: System.out.println(names.size()); then for (String name : names) { System.out.println(name); }

Why is ArrayList<Integer> used instead of ArrayList<int>?
options: Generics need reference types, not primitives
